overview:
Moses sets out what follows from obeying or refusing the LORD. If Israel hearkens, blessings will “overtake” them: blessed in city and field, in children, crops and herds, in coming and going; enemies scattered, rain in season, lending to nations and never borrowing, the head and not the tail. If Israel refuses, every blessing turns to a curse, and the list runs on for fifty more verses: disease, drought, defeat, madness, another man taking a man's wife, house and vineyard, exile with their king, a far nation whose siege drives parents to eat their children, and scattering among all peoples.

Watch where the curses end. The last threat is a return to Egypt in ships, to be offered as slaves where no one will buy (v. 68). Along the way come the “diseases of Egypt” (v. 60) and a people “left few in number” who had been as the stars (v. 62). Point by point, the Exodus runs backward.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Presented as Moses' speeches; the book says Moses wrote “this law” (31:9) and narrates his death. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars connect its core with the law book found under Josiah (2 Kings 22).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its core to the 7th century BC, with additions in the 6th.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Spoken in Moab in the fortieth year after the Exodus (1:3, 5). On the traditional Exodus date (about 1446 BC) that is about 1406 BC; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The plains of Moab. Moses speaks to Israel as one person, “thou,” warning of a land “whither thou goest to possess it” (vv. 21, 63).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Leviticus 26 (blessings and curses at Sinai, ending in remembrance of the covenant); Deuteronomy 11:26–28 (blessing and curse first set out). The Book of Mormon states a like covenant for its promised land (Ether 2:8–10).

hermeneutics:
Esarhaddon of Assyria made his vassals and officials swear loyalty to his heir in 672 BC, and the oath tablets end with a long run of curses. In one stretch, Sin clothes the oath-breaker with leprosy; Shamash takes away his eyesight so he walks about in darkness; Ninurta feeds his flesh to the eagle and vulture; and Venus makes his wife lie in his enemy's lap while strangers divide his goods and his sons lose his house. Verses 26–33 run through the same matters in nearly the same order: carrion birds, skin disease, blindness and groping in darkness, a betrothed wife taken, house, vineyard and herds seized, sons and daughters given to another people. Tigay notes that only the order is shared, and the wording differs too much to show copying; Crouch doubts any direct link. The striking change is that no gods are listed. In the treaty each god sends his own plague. Here “the LORD shall smite thee” covers them all.

In 2009 another copy of the same oath was found at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey, the seat of an Assyrian province. It lay in the inner room of a temple, beside a pedestal on which it seems to have been displayed. These oaths were sacred objects, kept before the gods. Judah was an Assyrian vassal in these years, and Assyrian lists of western kings bringing tribute include Manasseh of Judah; some scholars think he swore this very oath. Readers who knew such oaths would hear chapter 28 as a covenant of the same kind, with the LORD in the place of the great king and the law placed beside the ark as its witness (31:26).

breakdown.label: If thou hearken: the blessings shall overtake thee
Six “blessed” lines: city, field, offspring, basket, going
Victory, rain, plenty: the head and not the tail
If thou wilt not hearken: six “cursed” lines
Pestilence, drought, defeat, and the unburied dead
Disease, blindness, plunder, and exile with the king
Labor for nothing; the stranger above; a yoke of iron
A nation from far: siege and starvation
Plagues, scattering, and back to Egypt in ships

structure.summary: Parallel panels: each blessing (A–E) is answered by its curse (A′–E′), but the curse panel runs four times as long. Not a chiasm.

notes: **Proportion:** the blessings take 14 verses (vv. 1–14); the curses take 54 (vv. 15–68).
**Mirror lines:** “Blessed” (*baruk*) comes 6 times in vv. 3–6 and “cursed” (*arur*) 6 times in vv. 16–19, with the same subjects. The curses swap the middle two lines, basket before offspring.

**Refrain:** the curse panel keeps returning to destruction. The verb *shamad*, “destroy,” comes 7 times (vv. 20, 24, 45, 48, 51, 61, 63), most often in “until thou be destroyed.” Egypt is named 3 times (vv. 27, 60, 68).

Chapter 28 ends Moses' second address (4:44–28:68). The blessing and the curse were announced in 11:26–28 and staged on Gerizim and Ebal in chapter 27; here they are spelled out. The Hebrew Bible ends the chapter with one more verse (28:69), which the KJV prints as 29:1.

**Forward:** Daniel prays in Babylon that “the curse is poured upon us” as written in the law of Moses (Daniel 9:11). Moses himself answers the chapter in 30:1–3: when the blessing and the curse have both come, Israel can return and be gathered.

traditions.text: Nephi quotes the prophet Zenos on the people at Jerusalem who will turn their hearts aside and reject the God of Israel. They will wander in the flesh and perish, and “become a hiss and a byword, and be hated among all nations.” The wording follows v. 37, where Israel becomes an astonishment, a proverb and a byword among the nations. Zenos, a prophet known only from the brass plates, also foresees the scattered house of Israel remembered and gathered (1 Nephi 19:15–16), much as Deuteronomy 30 answers this chapter.

Abinadi's warning to King Noah's people draws on the same curses. They will be brought into bondage, smitten and slain, and “the vultures of the air, and the dogs” will devour their flesh. The Church's edition links the passage to v. 26, the carcass left to the birds and beasts with no one to frighten them away. Abinadi goes on to threaten famine, pestilence and the loss of crops to insects (Mosiah 12:4–7), much as vv. 21–22 and 38–42 do.

Moroni explains the decree for the Jaredites' promised land: whoever possesses it must serve God “or they shall be swept off” when they are ripened in iniquity. Like vv. 63–64, it ties a people's hold on a land to obedience and makes losing the land the final curse. The Book of Mormon applies the covenant pattern of this chapter to a second land and a second people, and Ether's closing chapters show it carried out.

The prophets of Jerusalem's fall reuse this chapter's words. Jeremiah threatens “a nation from far” whose language Judah will not understand, eating up its harvest and its flocks (compare vv. 49–51), and says the exiles will be removed into all the kingdoms of the earth and become a proverb, the words of vv. 25 and 37. Lamentations then reports that compassionate women boiled their own children in the siege, the horror of vv. 56–57 come true.

The exiles' confession in this apocryphal book says the Lord has confirmed his word against them. Nothing under heaven, they say, matches what was done in Jerusalem, where parents ate the flesh of their sons and daughters, just as the law of Moses had written. It reads the siege of vv. 53–57 as fulfilled in Babylon's siege of Jerusalem.

Writing after Rome had burned the temple, Josephus says Moses foretold it: if Israel broke the law, their land would be filled with enemy weapons, their cities overthrown, their temple burnt, and they would be sold as slaves to men with no pity. Yet God would restore the cities and the temple, and they would lose these things “not once only, but often.” He sets this prophecy among Moses' last speeches, beside the blessings and the song.

Abaye distinguishes the two curse chapters. Leviticus 26 is in the plural and Moses spoke it from the mouth of God, so its reading may not be split between readers; this chapter is in the singular and Moses said it on his own, so it may be. When one reader stammered over these curses, Rav Huna let him stop and another continue. A teaching credited to Ezra sets this chapter to be read before the New Year, so the year ends with its curses.

Argues that Leviticus 26 foretells the Babylonian exile and this chapter the Roman one. He points to the nation from far whose tongue Israel will not understand (v. 49), the scattering to the ends of the earth (v. 64), sons and daughters taken by another people (v. 32), and v. 68, fulfilled, he says, when Titus filled ships with captives. The Talmud's distinction between the two chapters becomes a distinction between two exiles. He adds that this chapter, unlike Leviticus 26, sets no end to the exile.

Reads the verb of v. 68 as reflexive: Israel will offer themselves for sale as slaves, and still no one will buy, because their enemies will have decreed their death. On this reading the last curse is worse than slavery, since even being bought would have meant survival.

Quotes v. 66 in a form close to the Hebrew, “your life shall be hanging before your eyes,” and adds that they would not believe their life. He reads it as Moses foretelling the Word, the one who made them, hanging on the tree while his own people did not believe in him. The KJV's “hang in doubt” hides the image this reading depends on.
